contradictions.question: Who may offer sacrifices to God?
contradictions.summary: The Priestly legislation in Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 restricts sacrifice to Aaronide priests at the tabernacle door, threatening death for any layperson who slaughters away from that one altar. But 1 Samuel happily reports Samuel — an Ephraimite, not a Levite — offering a burnt offering at Mizpah, and YHWH answers him without complaint.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization runs through Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties and Walter Kaiser's Hard Sayings. Their move is to argue that Samuel was a special case — a divinely commissioned prophet operating before the centralization at Jerusalem, that 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 retroactively makes Samuel a Levite by reckoning his line through Kohath, and that pre-temple sacrifice at high places was tolerated until Solomon's temple was built. Plenty of patriarchs offered sacrifices, the argument goes, so Samuel is just continuing that pattern in an unsettled period.

This harmonization has real exegetical weight on the high-places point. The Deuteronomistic Historian repeatedly notes that high-place sacrifice was tolerated "because the temple was not yet built" (1 Kings 3:2), and the genealogical retrojection in Chronicles is a known phenomenon. The problem is that the Numbers and Leviticus texts don't say "after the temple is built." Numbers 18:7 says any "stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death," and Leviticus 17:3-4 says any Israelite who slaughters in the camp or out of the camp without bringing it to the tabernacle door has "shed blood" and shall be "cut off from among his people." That's an unconditional death penalty, not a temporary measure.

The critical-scholarly read recognizes this as a classic source-critical fault line. Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 are Priestly material (P/H), reflecting a post-exilic ideology of cultic centralization with the Aaronide priesthood at the top. The Samuel narrative is older Deuteronomistic material that pre-dates that ideology and assumes a much more decentralized cult. Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena laid this out in 1878, and Israel Knohl's The Sanctuary of Silence has refined the dating but kept the basic insight: the Priestly source is projecting its own cultic vision back into Mosaic times. Samuel isn't violating the law — he's operating in a literary world where that law hasn't been imagined yet.

The Chronicler's Levite-Samuel move is itself good evidence that the post-exilic editors saw the problem and tried to paper over it. That is of course a subjective read of the editorial intent, but the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6 is hard to reconcile with the Ephraimite framing of 1 Samuel 1:1, which is the older text. Verdict: genuine contradiction, driven by competing source traditions about who could legitimately approach the altar.

contradictions.question: Is it necessary to keep the Sabbath?
contradictions.summary: The Torah and the prophets repeatedly insist the Sabbath is a perpetual sign of the covenant — Exodus 31:13-16 calls it an everlasting obligation and Isaiah 56:2 blesses anyone who keeps it. But Isaiah 1:13 has YHWH calling new moons and sabbath assemblies "iniquity" he can't stand.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic move here is contextual deflation. Geisler and Howe in When Critics Ask, along with most evangelical commentators, argue that Isaiah 1:13 isn't condemning Sabbath-keeping itself — it's condemning hypocritical Sabbath-keeping by people who oppress the poor the rest of the week. Read in context with verses 16-17 ("cease to do evil, learn to do well, seek judgment, relieve the oppressed"), the prophetic critique is targeting empty ritual without ethical substance, not the institution of Sabbath as such. This is the classic prophetic-cultic tension found across Amos 5, Hosea 6:6, and Micah 6:6-8.

This harmonization is actually the right read of Isaiah 1, and most critical scholars agree with it. John Goldingay, Joseph Blenkinsopp, and Brevard Childs all read 1:13 as rhetorical hyperbole condemning ritual divorced from justice, not as a repudiation of Sabbath itself. The contradiction at this level is genuinely weak — Isaiah is not a cessationist. So if we stop here, the entry doesn't really land.

But there is a sharper version of the same contradiction lurking in the New Testament that the SAB framing doesn't pick up. Paul in Colossians 2:16-17 explicitly tells believers not to let anyone judge them about "a sabbath day," calling it a shadow of things to come. Romans 14:5 makes Sabbath observance optional. Hebrews 4 spiritualizes it into eschatological rest. So when Christians cite Isaiah 56 to defend Sabbath while also citing Paul to dismiss it, they're stuck running both sides of the contradiction. The internal-Bible tension is real — it just isn't between Exodus and Isaiah, it's between the Torah/prophets and Pauline-Hebrews Christianity.

Verdict: weak as framed (Isaiah 1:13 is hyperbolic prophetic critique, not legal repeal), but a stronger version of the same contradiction exists between Torah Sabbath law and Pauline freedom from it. The SAB entry is undercooked.

contradictions.question: Should we judge others?
contradictions.summary: Jesus in Matthew 7:1 and Luke 6:37 commands his followers not to judge, and Paul echoes that in Romans 2:1 and 14:10 along with James 4:12. But Leviticus 19:15 commands righteous judgment of one's neighbor, John 7:24 has Jesus telling people to "judge righteous judgment," and Paul in 1 Corinthians 5-6 demands the Corinthians judge an immoral brother and even angels.
contradictions.commentary:
Note: the question field as scraped reads "Is God the author of confusion?" but the questionUrl (contra/judge.html) and all the citations are clearly about whether to judge others. The question text is wrong; the original SAB page is about judging. This commentary treats the actual contradiction in the answers.

The standard apologetic harmonization comes from D. A. Carson, R. T. France, and Craig Blomberg, all working the same line on Matthew 7:1. Jesus, they argue, is not forbidding all moral discernment — verses 6 and 15 of the same chapter command discernment about "dogs," "swine," and false prophets, which presupposes judgment. The Greek krino can mean "condemn" as well as "evaluate," and Matthew 7:1 is targeting hypocritical, censorious condemnation, not careful moral evaluation. That's why John 7:24 can simultaneously say "judge not by appearance" and "judge righteous judgment" — different senses of the verb. Paul's "judge nothing before the time" in 1 Corinthians 4:5 is specifically about ultimate eschatological verdicts on motives, while 1 Corinthians 5:12 is about present-tense church discipline of obvious public sin.

This harmonization is actually pretty good. The Greek krino does have semantic range, and the Matthean and Pauline contexts do support a distinction between condemnatory judgment (forbidden) and discerning evaluation (commanded). Davies and Allison in their ICC Matthew defend this read, as does Anthony Thiselton on 1 Corinthians. So the surface-level contradiction softens significantly when you do the lexical work.

Where it doesn't fully dissolve is at the level of moral consistency. Matthew 7:1-2 doesn't just say "don't be a hypocrite" — it grounds the prohibition on the principle that the measure you use will be used against you, which is a universal rule, not a niche rule about hypocrites. And 1 Corinthians 5:3-5 has Paul "having judged already" the immoral brother and demanding the church hand him over to Satan — that's not gentle discernment, that's a verdict pronounced from a distance on a single report. The same Paul who tells the Romans not to judge their brother (14:10) is judging brothers in Corinth from Ephesus. Dale Allison in The Sermon on the Mount notes the tension between Jesus' radical prohibition and the church's practical need for discipline, and grants that the early communities were already negotiating it.

Verdict: weak-to-moderate contradiction. The Greek lexical range and immediate context resolve most of the surface tension, but a residual ethical inconsistency remains in how Paul applies the principle. Mostly a translation-and-context issue rather than a hard textual contradiction.

contradictions.question: Should we love or hate our brother?
contradictions.summary: Jesus in Luke 14:26 says no one can be his disciple unless they hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even their own life. Leviticus 19:17-18 forbids hating your brother in your heart and commands loving your neighbor as yourself, and 1 John 3:15 calls anyone who hates his brother a murderer with no eternal life in him.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic move here is the Semitic-idiom defense, deployed by D. A. Carson, Darrell Bock, and pretty much every evangelical Lukan commentator. The Aramaic miseo or Hebrew sane often functions in a comparative sense — "love less than" — and Matthew 10:37 preserves what looks like the same saying with that softer phrasing: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Genesis 29:31 says Leah was "hated" while Jacob "loved" Rachel, but the next verse and the broader narrative show Leah was simply less-loved, not despised. So Luke 14:26, on this read, isn't a literal command to hate family — it's hyperbolic Semitic comparison demanding that loyalty to Jesus outrank every other tie.

This harmonization has substantial scholarly backing. Joseph Fitzmyer in his Anchor Bible Luke and François Bovon in his Hermeneia Luke both acknowledge the Semitic comparative function of miseo here. Matthew's version really does look like a softening of the same Q tradition, suggesting Matthew himself or his community already heard the absoluteness of "hate" as needing rephrasing. So at the lexical level, the contradiction softens significantly.

Where it doesn't fully dissolve is the rhetorical and theological force of the saying. Even if miseo means "love less," Jesus is still demanding a level of family-rejection that Leviticus 19 and 1 John 4:20-21 frame as incompatible with the love commandment. John Meier in A Marginal Jew (especially the family-relations material in Volume One) argues the historical Jesus really did demand a radical break with kinship structures — that's the whole "let the dead bury their dead" pattern in Matthew 8:22, the rejection of his mother and brothers in Mark 3:31-35, the family-against-family prediction in Matthew 10:34-36. The early Jesus movement appears to have been genuinely disruptive of household ties, and the SAB contradiction picks up on that real tension. Meanwhile 1 John 3:15 makes hating one's brother literally murderous — there's no semantic softening that gets you from "hate father and mother" to "love father and mother as yourself" without doing some interpretive labor.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The Semitic comparative reading partly resolves the surface tension, but the deeper moral-theological tension between Jesus' kinship-disrupting demands and the Levitical-Johannine love ethic is real. Apologists are right that miseo is hyperbolic; critics are right that the underlying ethic still pulls against the love commandment when you stop softening the Greek.

contradictions.question: How should nonbelievers be treated?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 13:6-10 commands the execution by stoning of any family member who entices Israel to follow other gods. 2 Corinthians 6:14-17 says to separate from unbelievers and have no fellowship with them. But the same Bible commands love of neighbor and even love of enemies in Leviticus 19:18, Matthew 5:44, and Luke 6:27.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here works the dispensational and contextual angles. Norman Geisler, Paul Copan in Is God a Moral Monster?, and Christopher Wright in The God I Don't Understand all argue that Deuteronomy 13 is a unique theocratic statute for ancient Israel as a covenant-bound nation, not a perpetual ethical norm. Israel under the Sinai covenant was a holy nation set apart for cultic purity, and apostasy was treason against the covenant suzerain — comparable to ancient Near Eastern vassal-treaty stipulations. The new covenant in Christ, on this read, replaces civil enforcement with persuasion, which is why Jesus and Paul shift to love-of-enemy ethics.

This dispensational move has genuine support in the structure of the canon — Deuteronomy is covenant law for a specific theocratic polity, and the apostolic writings repeatedly distinguish church discipline from civil enforcement. Bernard Levinson and Jeffrey Tigay both note the ancient Near Eastern parallels in Hittite and Neo-Assyrian vassal treaties (especially the Vassal Treaties of Esarhaddon), where treason against the suzerain warrants death. So Deuteronomy 13 fits a known genre. The 2 Corinthians passage about unequal yoking is also genuinely about cultic separation, not about hostility.

Where the harmonization runs into trouble is the moral-philosophical level. If "thou shalt surely kill him; thine hand shall be first upon him" was ever the right ethical response to a family member's religious dissent, then the moral standard has either changed or it was never absolute. Either way, the unified-divine-character claim takes a hit. C. S. Cowles in Show Them No Mercy concedes this and goes the marcionite-adjacent route of saying Jesus reveals what God is really like and the Deuteronomic herem reflects accommodation to Iron Age categories. Eric Seibert in Disturbing Divine Behavior makes the same move more aggressively. The cost of that move is admitting the Deuteronomic author got God wrong, which is a significant theological concession. Christopher Wright tries to hold both — Deuteronomy 13 was right then, the cross is right now — but that leaves you with a God whose ethics are situationally relative.

Verdict: genuine contradiction at the ethical level, partially masked by canonical-covenantal framing. The dispensational defense saves the texts from direct contradiction but only by conceding that what counts as faithful treatment of nonbelievers shifted radically — which is its own theological problem.

contradictions.question: How should adulterers be punished?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 20:10 commands the execution of both the adulterer and the adulteress. The pericope adulterae in John 7:53-8:11 has Jesus refuse to condemn a woman caught in adultery and instead invite the sinless to throw the first stone — effectively suspending the death penalty.
contradictions.commentary:
There are actually two separate problems with this contradiction, and the textual one is bigger than the apologetic harmonization.

Problem one: the pericope adulterae is almost certainly not original to John's Gospel. It's missing from the earliest and best manuscripts — Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus — and shows up in different locations in later manuscripts (sometimes in Luke, sometimes elsewhere in John). Bruce Metzger's Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament gives it the rare double-bracket treatment, and the NA28 critical apparatus excludes it from the main text. Bart Ehrman in Misquoting Jesus and Chris Keith in The Pericope Adulterae, the Gospel of John, and the Literacy of Jesus both accept the manuscript verdict: the story is a free-floating oral tradition that got inserted into John in the medieval period. So citing it against Leviticus 20:10 is citing a text most critical scholars consider a later interpolation. That's a textual-critical problem the SAB framing ignores.

Problem two, granting that the pericope was written sometime by someone: the standard apologetic harmonization comes from D. A. Carson, who points out that Jesus didn't actually overturn the Mosaic penalty — he just exposed the legal-procedural defect in the case (Deuteronomy 17:7 requires witnesses to cast the first stone, and the witnesses here had unclean hands, possibly literally if the man wasn't dragged in alongside her). On this read, Jesus is operating within the law, not against it. Andreas Köstenberger in his BECNT John runs a similar version of this argument. It's a defensible read of the narrative as it stands.

But even granting Carson's read, there's a remainder. Jesus doesn't say "this case has procedural defects, retry it with proper witnesses." He says "neither do I condemn thee." That's a refusal to apply the penalty, not just a delay. And the story functions in Christian tradition precisely as a softening of Levitical severity. James Dunn in Jesus Remembered notes that whatever the historical Jesus said about adultery (Matthew 5:27-30 ratchets the Mosaic standard up internally rather than abolishing the external penalty), the cultural memory of Jesus that produced the pericope was already moving away from execution.

Verdict: structurally moderate but textually weak. The contradiction depends on a passage most critical scholars consider non-original to John. If you grant the passage, the harmonization is reasonable but doesn't fully erase the softening of the death penalty. The honest answer is that early Christianity, whoever wrote the pericope, was already abandoning Levitical execution for adultery — that itself is the contradiction with Torah law.

contradictions.question: How should homosexuals be treated?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 20:13 prescribes the death penalty for male same-sex intercourse. 1 Kings 15:11-12 reports Asa simply removing the qedeshim (translated "sodomites" in the KJV) from the land, which reads as exile rather than execution.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction looks sharper in English than it does in Hebrew, and the standard apologetic harmonization works that gap. The KJV "sodomites" in 1 Kings 15:12 translates qedeshim, literally "holy ones" — a term most critical scholars now recognize as referring to cultic functionaries associated with Canaanite or syncretistic worship, not specifically to homosexual practice. Phyllis Bird and Mayer Gruber have argued in detail that the older identification of qedeshim with male temple prostitutes engaged in same-sex acts is overdetermined by the LXX and by KJV translators reading their own categories back into the text. The qedeshim are religious-office holders being expelled from a syncretistic cult, not a category equivalent to the men described in Leviticus 20:13.

This textual point genuinely undercuts the sharp form of the contradiction. Apologists from Robert Gagnon (The Bible and Homosexual Practice) to more critical scholars like John Boswell agree that 1 Kings 15:12 is doing something different from Leviticus 20:13. So if the question is "do these two texts disagree about how to punish gay people," the answer is partly that they're not even talking about the same thing — the Leviticus text targets a sex act, the Kings text targets a cultic role.

The residual problem, though, is that ancient Israel as represented in the Deuteronomistic History never actually carries out Leviticus 20:13. Across Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, you don't find a single execution of an Israelite for same-sex intercourse. Asa removes the qedeshim, Josiah breaks down their houses (2 Kings 23:7), and the pattern is consistently expulsion or destruction of cultic infrastructure rather than capital punishment of individuals for the sex act per se. Jacob Milgrom in his Anchor Bible Leviticus argues the Holiness Code's death penalty was more rhetorical-legislative than judicially enforced; the broader scholarly observation that biblical capital statutes rarely show evidence of actual enforcement is also developed by Bernard Jackson and others. So the contradiction the SAB framing is reaching for — between the lethal Levitical statute and the milder narrative response — is real, but the qedeshim/sodomite mistranslation is the wrong textual hook for it.

Verdict: weak as cited because of the translation problem. There is a genuine tension between the Holiness Code's death penalty and the Deuteronomistic History's actual practice, but 1 Kings 15:12 isn't the verse that demonstrates it. The entry as scraped relies on a KJV translation artifact that modern critical scholarship has largely abandoned.

contradictions.question: How should a man who has sex with a menstruating woman be punished?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 15:24 says a man who has sex with a menstruating woman is unclean for seven days, with no further consequence. Leviticus 20:18 says both he and the woman "shall be cut off from among their people" — a severe penalty, often understood as karet, divine excision.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a clean source-critical contradiction within the book of Leviticus itself, and the apologetic harmonizations have to do real work to dissolve it. The standard move from Gleason Archer and from R. K. Harrison's Tyndale Leviticus is to argue that the two texts describe different scenarios: Leviticus 15:24 covers an inadvertent case where the man didn't know the woman was menstruating, while 20:18 covers the deliberate act where "he hath discovered her fountain." The verb galah ("uncover") in 20:18 supposedly implies intentional exposure, while 15:24 covers accidental contact.

This read isn't crazy. The Mishnah (Keritot 1:1-2) and later rabbinic interpretation already recognized the tension and tried to resolve it along similar lines, distinguishing accidental from willful niddah-violation within the karet-offense framework. Jacob Milgrom in his Anchor Bible Leviticus 17-22 acknowledges this rabbinic tradition. So apologists aren't inventing the distinction from scratch.

What the harmonization can't fully escape is the source-critical evidence that Leviticus 15 and Leviticus 20 belong to different sources within the Priestly material. Leviticus 15 is part of the older Priestly purity code (P), which treats menstrual contact as a ritual-impurity issue handled by waiting periods and washing. Leviticus 20 belongs to the Holiness Code (H), which Israel Knohl and Jacob Milgrom argue is a later expansion that systematically ratchets up Priestly penalties — turning ritual-impurity matters into capital-or-karet offenses. Knohl in The Sanctuary of Silence makes this exact point: H takes P's purity rules and reframes them as moral-covenantal violations punishable by excision. The two texts aren't talking about "different scenarios" — they're two different legal traditions on the same scenario, with H trying to escalate P's penalty. The harmonizing distinction between accidental and intentional has no textual marker in 15:24 itself; nothing in that verse signals inadvertence. It's read in to save the consistency.

The early rabbinic tradition (cf. Mishnah Keritot 1:1-2 listing intercourse with a niddah among the karet offenses, with attendant Gemara discussion of inadvertent vs. intentional violation) explicitly raises the contradiction and resolves it the apologetic way, but that's exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization Knohl identifies as covering over the underlying source seam. Verdict: genuine contradiction, partially resolvable by reading inadvertence into 15:24, but cleanly explained by the H-redacts-P source theory. The harmonization works only if you stipulate a distinction the texts don't make.

contradictions.question: Does God love everyone?
contradictions.summary: John 3:16 says God so loved the world, and 1 John 4:8 and 4:16 declare God is love. But the Hebrew Bible has YHWH explicitly hating nations, the wicked, the workers of iniquity, false witnesses, the disobedient, and Esau by name — and Romans 9:13 picks up that last one as canonical New Testament theology.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization comes in two flavors. The first, from John MacArthur, John Piper, and the broader Reformed camp, is to distinguish God's general benevolent love for creation from his special covenantal love for the elect. On this read, God can "love the world" in John 3:16 in the sense of general kindness or providential care while simultaneously hating Esau in the sense of preterition — passing him over for elective covenant love. D. A. Carson's The Difficult Doctrine of the Love of God develops this with five distinct senses of divine love. The second flavor, from Walter Kaiser and others working on the Hebrew, is the Semitic-comparative move: "hate" in Malachi 1:3 and Romans 9:13 means "love less" or "reject as covenant heir," not literal emotional hatred — the same idiom we saw in Luke 14:26 about hating father and mother.

Both moves have real textual warrant. The Semitic comparative use of sane/miseo is well-documented (Genesis 29:31, Deuteronomy 21:15-17). And Carson is right that biblical love-language operates in multiple registers. James Dunn in his Romans 9-16 commentary and Douglas Moo in his NICNT Romans both note that Paul in Romans 9:13 is not making a claim about God's emotional state toward Esau the individual, but about election of Jacob over Esau as nations.

Where this runs into trouble is the texts the SAB cites that aren't using comparative-language at all. Psalm 5:5 says God hates (sane) all workers of iniquity. Psalm 11:5 says he hates the wicked and the lover of violence. Hosea 9:15 has YHWH say "I hated them" about Israel itself. Leviticus 20:23 has him "abhorring" the Canaanites. None of these are Jacob-Esau elective contrasts; they're straightforward statements of divine antipathy toward categories of people. Patrick Miller in *Interpreting the Psalms* and other major psalms scholars note the language of divine hatred in the Hebrew Bible is morally charged, not just relational shorthand. Meanwhile, the unconditional 1 John 4:8 "God is love" is an ontological identification, not a description of one mode among many.

The Reformed harmonization preserves both texts at the cost of saying God loves and hates the same person in different senses simultaneously, which only works if you accept the prior framework. The Semitic-comparative read works for Romans 9:13 but not for the Psalmist's hate-the-wicked passages. Verdict: genuine contradiction at the level of biblical-theological coherence. The texts represent different theological streams — the Deuteronomic-Wisdom hate-the-wicked tradition versus the Johannine universalist God-is-love tradition — that have to be harmonized rather than read together naturally.

contradictions.question: May a eunuch enter into the congregation of the Lord?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 23:1 explicitly bars anyone with crushed testicles or a severed penis from the assembly of YHWH. Leviticus 21:17-21 bars Aaronide priests with physical blemishes from offering sacrifice. But Isaiah 56:3-5 promises eunuchs a place and a name in YHWH's house "better than of sons and of daughters" — directly addressing and reversing the Deuteronomic exclusion.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner intra-canonical contradictions in the Hebrew Bible, and even most apologists acknowledge tension here. The standard harmonization runs along progressive-revelation or different-contexts lines: Deuteronomy 23 was for the wilderness/conquest-era covenant assembly when ritual purity of the polity was paramount, Leviticus 21 covers a narrower category (priests offering sacrifice, not all eunuchs), and Isaiah 56 is announcing an eschatological reversal as part of the prophetic vision of the new covenant. Joseph Blenkinsopp in his Anchor Bible Isaiah 56-66 reads it this way; so does Brevard Childs in his Old Testament Library Isaiah commentary.

The progressive-revelation read isn't wrong as far as it goes. Isaiah 56 self-consciously addresses and overturns the Deuteronomic exclusion — it's a polemical reversal, not a separate topic. The text knows what it's contradicting and does it on purpose. Brevard Childs and Walter Brueggemann both note that Trito-Isaiah is engaged in a deliberate re-opening of the boundaries of YHWH's people that the Deuteronomic and Priestly traditions had drawn tightly.

Where the harmonization stops working is when you ask whether Deuteronomy 23 was right when it was written. If "no man with crushed testicles shall enter the assembly" was YHWH's word at Moab, then Isaiah is announcing a change in divine policy. If it wasn't right when it was written, then the Deuteronomist got God wrong. Either you have a God whose ethics evolve (which the divine-immutability claim of classical theism rejects) or you have a contradicting human tradition. The Christian appropriation of Isaiah 56 in Acts 8 with the Ethiopian eunuch implicitly chooses the first option, but the cost is admitting the Mosaic exclusion was provisional rather than absolute. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible argues this is the basic structure of biblical theology: later texts engaging earlier texts to revise them, with the editorial framing pretending continuity. Bernard Levinson's Legal Revision and Religious Renewal in Ancient Israel makes the case in detail for Deuteronomy itself doing this to earlier law, and Trito-Isaiah does it again to Deuteronomy.

Verdict: genuine contradiction, openly acknowledged by Isaiah 56 itself as a reversal of Deuteronomic policy. The progressive-revelation harmonization saves the texts from direct collision but only by conceding that the criteria for belonging to YHWH's people changed substantively over time.

contradictions.question: Should you punish people with an eye for eye and a tooth for a tooth?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 24:19-20 codifies the lex talionis: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, breach for breach. Matthew 5:38-39 has Jesus directly quote that statute and overturn it: "But I say unto you, that ye resist not evil."
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here, deployed by R. T. France, D. A. Carson, and Craig Blomberg, is to argue that Jesus isn't abolishing lex talionis as a civil-judicial principle — he's correcting its misapplication as a personal-ethics principle. Leviticus 24, on this read, was always intended as a courtroom standard for proportional justice (and notably as a limiting principle, capping retribution at parity rather than escalating it), while the Pharisees of Jesus' day had wrongly extended it to govern personal vengeance. So Jesus' "resist not evil" addresses interpersonal ethics, not civil law. R. T. France's NICNT Matthew makes this argument in detail; Mathew Henry was making it three centuries earlier.

This harmonization has substantial scholarly grounding. Jacob Milgrom and Bernard Jackson both point out that lex talionis in Leviticus 24 is almost certainly a limiting principle — capping retribution rather than mandating it — and likely functioned in practice through monetary compensation rather than literal mutilation. Cuneiform parallels in Hammurabi and the Hittite laws show this kind of statute typically operated as a maximum, not a minimum. So Jesus' Matthean correction of the Pharisaic application has a real target.

Where the harmonization stops working is the rhetorical force of Matthew 5:38-39 itself. Jesus structures the antithesis as "You have heard that it was said... but I say unto you," which sets his teaching against, not alongside, the cited statute. The cited statute is Leviticus, not a Pharisaic misapplication. Hans Dieter Betz in his Hermeneia Sermon on the Mount argues the antitheses don't simply correct misinterpretations — they offer a higher righteousness that goes beyond Torah, in some cases revising Torah itself. Ulrich Luz in his Hermeneia Matthew acknowledges that Matthew 5:38-39 raises a real question about whether Jesus is abolishing or fulfilling, and notes that the church has been negotiating that ambiguity since the second century. Marcion read these antitheses as Jesus replacing the Mosaic law; the Reformers read them as Jesus deepening it; both readings are textually defensible.

Meanwhile Matthew 5:17-18 has Jesus say he hasn't come to abolish the law, which makes the antitheses internally tense even within the Sermon on the Mount itself. So the contradiction is partly within Matthew, partly between Matthew and Leviticus. Verdict: moderate contradiction. The civil-vs-personal distinction softens the surface tension, but the antithetical structure of Matthew 5 makes a straightforward harmonization difficult, and Jesus appears to be moving the moral standard somewhere lex talionis didn't go.

contradictions.question: Should we fear God?
contradictions.summary: The Torah, prophets, and Wisdom literature relentlessly command fear of YHWH — Deuteronomy 6:13, Ecclesiastes 12:13, Proverbs 9:10, Matthew 10:28, and Hebrews 10:31 all insist on it. But 1 John 4:18 says perfect love casts out fear, 2 Timothy 1:7 says God didn't give us a spirit of fear, and Romans 8:15 says believers haven't received a spirit of bondage to fear.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here is the two-senses-of-fear move, deployed by John Calvin, Wayne Grudem, and basically every systematic theology written since the Reformation. Hebrew yirah and Greek phobos cover a semantic range from "reverential awe" to "terror." The fear commanded in Proverbs 9:10 ("the fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom") is reverential — submissive awe before the Creator — while the fear cast out by 1 John 4:18 is the servile dread of punishment that Christ's atonement removes. So believers fear God in sense 1 (awe) and don't fear God in sense 2 (terror). C. S. Lewis works this distinction in The Problem of Pain; D. A. Carson develops it in his Difficult Doctrine of the Love of God.

This lexical move is genuine. Yirah does have semantic range — Bruce Waltke in his NICOT Proverbs and Michael Fox in his Anchor Bible Proverbs both confirm that the wisdom-tradition's "fear of YHWH" is heavily weighted toward reverential submission, not panic. And 1 John 4:18 specifically links the fear that's cast out with kolasis — punishment, torment — which suggests servile dread. So the two-senses harmonization has real textual purchase on the wisdom-literature passages.

Where the harmonization runs into trouble is the Synoptic and Hebrews passages the SAB cites. Matthew 10:28 ("fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell") and Hebrews 10:31 ("a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God") aren't talking about reverential awe — they're talking about the prospect of divine punishment, which is exactly what 1 John 4:18 says perfect love casts out. So the harmonization that works for Proverbs doesn't work for Matthew 10:28. Either Matthew 10:28 is commanding the dread of punishment that 1 John 4:18 says love eliminates, or Matthew 10:28 is also somehow reverential — but "destroy soul and body in hell" makes that read strained. Luke Timothy Johnson and Raymond Brown both note this internal NT tension between the fear-stoking passages of the Synoptics and Hebrews and the love-perfecting passages of Johannine and Pauline material.

There's also the prosperity-gospel residue in the Wisdom passages the SAB cites: Proverbs 22:4 says fearing YHWH brings riches and honor, Proverbs 19:23 says the God-fearer won't be visited with evil — claims the book of Job and Ecclesiastes themselves push back against. So the contradiction isn't just between Hebrew Bible and New Testament; it's also within the Hebrew Bible's own wisdom dialogue.

Verdict: moderate-to-strong contradiction. The two-senses move handles the reverential-awe passages but doesn't get rid of the Synoptic and Hebrews passages that are clearly about dread of punishment, which 1 John 4:18 explicitly says love removes.

contradictions.question: Did God tell Moses to number the Levites?
contradictions.summary: Numbers 1:48-49 records YHWH explicitly telling Moses NOT to number the tribe of Levi among the children of Israel, and Numbers 2:33 confirms the Levites were not numbered as commanded. But Numbers 3:14-15 has YHWH then telling Moses to number the Levites by their fathers' houses, every male a month old and upward.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here is straightforward and substantially correct: the two commands are about two different censuses. Numbers 1 is the military census of fighting men aged twenty and upward, from which the Levites are excluded because their job is the tabernacle, not warfare. Numbers 3 is a separate Levitical census specifically for sanctuary service, counting every male from one month old. So the Levites aren't excluded from all counting — they're excluded from the military count and given their own dedicated count. Gleason Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Roy Gane in his NIVAC Numbers, and Timothy Ashley in his NICOT Numbers all run this argument and they're not wrong.

The text itself supports the harmonization. Numbers 1:3 specifies the count is "every male... from twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war," and 1:48-49 says "only thou shalt not number the tribe of Levi." The exclusion is from the military count, not from all counting. Numbers 3:14-15 then gives a separate command with different parameters (one month and upward) for a different purpose (sanctuary service and substitution for the firstborn of Israel). The two censuses serve different functions and have different age brackets, which is exactly what you'd expect if they were genuinely separate procedures rather than contradictory commands.

Where there's still room for source-critical interest is the broader question of why Numbers preserves so many overlapping and partially-redundant census materials at all. Baruch Levine in his Anchor Bible Numbers notes the layered Priestly redaction visible across Numbers 1-4 and 26, and Thomas Dozeman has argued some of these counts reflect different documentary stages. But that's a question about the composition of Numbers, not about a logical contradiction between 1:48-49 and 3:14-15 as the text now stands.

Verdict: weak contradiction. The two commands address different censuses with different criteria and different purposes, and the text marks the distinction clearly. The SAB framing only works if you flatten the two counts into one, which the text resists. This is a case where the apologetic harmonization is genuinely the better read.

contradictions.question: How many male Levites more than one month old did Moses and Aaron count?
contradictions.summary: Numbers 3:39 gives the total of all male Levites a month old and upward as 22,000. But the same chapter breaks the count into clans — 7,500 Gershonites (3:22), 8,600 Kohathites (3:28), and 6,200 Merarites (3:34) — which sums to 22,300, not 22,000. The 300-Levite gap is internal to a single chapter.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a genuine arithmetic problem internal to Numbers 3, and the apologetic harmonization tradition has been working it for centuries. The standard move from Keil and Delitzsch onward, picked up by Gleason Archer and Timothy Ashley in NICOT Numbers, is the firstborn-deduction theory. Numbers 3:40-51 has YHWH command Moses to use the Levites as a substitution for the firstborn of all Israel, and there are 22,273 firstborn Israelites (3:43). The deal is one Levite per firstborn, with a 5-shekel redemption fee for the surplus 273 firstborn. For that exchange to work, the apologetic argument runs, the 300 Levites in question must themselves be firstborn — they can't redeem someone else's firstborn status because they already have their own. So the round 22,000 number in 3:39 represents Levites available for substitution, with 300 firstborn Levites excluded from that count.

This explanation has the virtue of using the immediate context to solve the problem, and it's not crazy. Numbers 3:40-51 is clearly thinking about firstborn-Levite substitution and a 273-firstborn surplus does need to be redeemed somehow. But the explanation has two significant problems. First, the text doesn't say this. Numbers 3:39 says "all that were numbered of the Levites... were twenty and two thousand," which on a plain reading is the total count, not a substitution-eligible subset. The harmonization requires reading an unstated qualification into the verse. Second, the 300-firstborn-Levites number is itself stipulated to make the math work — there's no independent textual evidence that exactly 300 Levite firstborn existed.

More importantly, the critical-scholarly take recognizes this as one of many internal numerical inconsistencies that betray Numbers' compositional history. Baruch Levine and Jacob Milgrom both note that the Priestly census materials contain numbers that don't always reconcile, suggesting either scribal corruption in transmission (textual critics like Emanuel Tov flag exactly this kind of round-number/sum mismatch as common) or layered redaction where the clan figures and the round total come from different sources. The Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch both preserve the same numbers, so the corruption (if that's what it is) is pre-LXX.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The firstborn-Levites apologetic move is clever and contextually motivated, but it's an unstated qualification read into 3:39 specifically to save the math. The simpler explanation is that Numbers 3 contains an arithmetic problem the redactors either didn't notice or didn't care about — which itself tells you something about how the text was transmitted.

contradictions.question: How old did a Levite have to be to be counted?
contradictions.summary: Numbers 4:3 sets the age of Levitical service at thirty to fifty years old. Numbers 8:24 lowers it to twenty-five. Ezra 3:8, 1 Chronicles 23:24, 23:27, and 2 Chronicles 31:17 lower it again to twenty.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here is the apprenticeship-and-historical-development theory, deployed by Gleason Archer, Walter Kaiser in Hard Sayings of the Bible, and Edwin Yamauchi. The argument runs that 25-30 was an apprenticeship period before full service at 30 (Numbers 8:24-26 has the 25-year-olds doing some kind of waiting/assisting work), and the post-exilic Chronicler texts reflect a different historical situation: David, knowing the temple work would be different from tabernacle work (lighter physical demands once the structure was permanent), lowered the age to 20. So the numbers don't contradict — they describe an evolving institution responding to changing circumstances. The Talmud b. Hullin 24a already raises this question and runs a similar harmonization.

The development theory is actually plausible at a high level. It's not unreasonable to think that Israel's cultic personnel rules changed between the wilderness period and the post-exilic period, and 1 Chronicles 23:25-27 explicitly attributes the lowered age to David's recognition that the Levites no longer needed to carry the tabernacle. So there is a textual hook for the harmonization. Sara Japhet's I and II Chronicles in the Old Testament Library notes that the Chronicler is openly reworking earlier Levitical legislation to fit the post-exilic temple economy.

Where it stops fully working is the Numbers 4:3 vs. Numbers 8:24 problem within the same book. Both texts purport to be Mosaic legislation given in the wilderness, and the apprenticeship-vs-full-service distinction is a harmonization that has to be read into 8:24, which simply says "from twenty and five years old and upward they shall go in to wait upon the service." The Hebrew lavo letsava ha-tsava is the same language used for active service in 4:3, just with a different age. Baruch Levine in his Anchor Bible Numbers and Jacob Milgrom both treat Numbers 4 and 8 as belonging to slightly different P-redactional layers reflecting different practical needs, with 4 likely earlier and 8 a later modification. So even before you get to Chronicles, there's a Priestly-internal disagreement.

The Chronicler's lowering to 20 is the cleanest case of the post-exilic community openly adjusting Mosaic legislation, and Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson both note this is an admission that the Mosaic age requirements weren't permanent. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible reads this kind of intra-canonical revision as standard biblical practice — later editors updating earlier texts and pretending continuity.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The development-of-institutions defense works for the Numbers-vs-Chronicles tension if you grant that Mosaic legislation could be revised. The apprenticeship theory for Numbers 4 vs. Numbers 8 is more strained — it requires reading a distinction into 8:24 that the text doesn't make. The honest reading is that Israel's cultic legislation changed over time and the canonical text preserves all the layers without harmonizing them.

contradictions.question: Is it OK for men to have long hair?
contradictions.summary: The Nazirite vow in Numbers 6:5 forbids razors and commands the locks of the head to grow — Samson and Samuel are the famous examples. But 1 Corinthians 11:14 says nature itself teaches that long hair on a man is a shame to him, and Ezekiel 44:20 forbids priests from letting their locks grow long.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here is the special-vow-vs-general-norm distinction, deployed by Gordon Fee in his NICNT 1 Corinthians, Anthony Thiselton in his NIGTC 1 Corinthians, and Daniel Block in his NICOT Ezekiel. The Nazirite vow was a temporary, voluntary consecration that suspended ordinary cultural norms about hair as a visible sign of dedication. So the long hair of a Nazirite is precisely a religious marker — it's set apart from normal practice. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11 is talking about ordinary cultural practice in Corinthian worship, where long male hair carried very different connotations (often associated with effeminacy or pederastic culture in the Greco-Roman world). Ezekiel 44:20 governs Zadokite priests during temple service, which is yet another distinct context.

This harmonization works pretty well at the surface level. The texts are addressing different social roles — temporary vow-takers, ordinary Corinthian worshippers, Zadokite priests — and each has different hair conventions. Bruce Winter in After Paul Left Corinth and Cynthia Thompson in her work on Roman hair culture have shown how thoroughly hair styling was coded in first-century Mediterranean society, and Paul's argument from "nature" (physis) probably appeals to Greco-Roman cultural categories his Corinthian audience would have shared. So the apparent contradiction softens significantly when you situate each passage in its social context.

Where the harmonization gets weaker is Paul's actual argument. He doesn't say "in your culture long hair is shameful" — he says "doth not even nature itself teach you." Physis here is being deployed as a universal claim, not a culturally-relative one. Wayne Meeks in The First Urban Christians and Dale Martin in The Corinthian Body both engage Paul's appeal to physis, with Martin reading it through ancient physiological categories rather than as a culturally-relative claim. If physis really does teach this, then it should have taught the same to Israel in Numbers 6 and to the Nazirites Samson and Samuel — but it didn't. Either Paul is wrong about what nature teaches, or nature taught different things to different cultures, or the Nazirite vow overrides natural revelation. None of those are great options for a unified-Bible reading.

Meanwhile, Absalom's hair is a plot point that's celebrated in 2 Samuel 14:25-26, and several biblical heroes are hairy. The cultural coding of long male hair varied across biblical periods and contexts, and the canonical text preserves the variation without resolving it.

Verdict: weak-to-moderate contradiction. The contextual harmonization handles most of the tension if you accept that hair conventions varied across roles and periods. The remainder is Paul's universalizing "nature" argument, which doesn't sit cleanly with Numbers 6 if both are revealing the same divine perspective on hair.

contradictions.question: Who wrote the Pentateuch?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 31:9 and 1:1 attribute the Mosaic law to Moses, and the historical Christian and Jewish position has been Mosaic authorship of the entire Pentateuch. But Numbers 12:3 calls Moses the meekest man on the face of the earth — a claim it would be bizarre for Moses to write about himself — and Deuteronomy 34 narrates Moses' death, also implausibly self-authored.
contradictions.commentary:
The SAB framing is unusually weak here, because the Numbers 12:3 "meekest man" verse is one of the smaller arrows in the quiver against Mosaic authorship. The big problems are the post-Mosaic geographical and historical references (Genesis 12:6 "the Canaanite was then in the land," Genesis 36:31 "before any king reigned over the children of Israel," Numbers 21:14 quoting the Book of the Wars of YHWH as a separate source), the death and burial of Moses in Deuteronomy 34, the linguistic features that point to first-millennium rather than Late Bronze Age Hebrew, and the documentary evidence of multiple sources interwoven across the Pentateuch.

The traditional defense of Mosaic authorship, made by Gleason Archer in his Survey of Old Testament Introduction and Duane Garrett in Rethinking Genesis, runs three main moves. First, the post-Mosaic notices are minor scribal updatings — later editors clarifying place names for contemporary readers. Second, Numbers 12:3's "meekest man" is either a parenthetical insertion by a later editor (Joshua, traditionally) or simply Moses transcribing what God said about him under prophetic inspiration. Third, Deuteronomy 34 was added after Moses' death by his successor; Talmud b. Bava Batra 14b-15a already proposes Joshua wrote the last eight verses. So Mosaic authorship can be retained with minor caveats.

The critical-scholarly position is the Documentary Hypothesis or its descendants. Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena and the subsequent JEDP framework identifies four main sources: J (Yahwist), E (Elohist), D (Deuteronomist), and P (Priestly), woven together by post-exilic redactors. The evidence is not just "meekest man" — it's the doublets (two creation accounts, two flood narratives, three wife-sister episodes), the differing divine names, the contradictory legal codes (Exodus 20-23 vs. Deuteronomy 12-26 vs. the Priestly material in Leviticus), and the differing theologies. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible and Joel Baden in The Composition of the Pentateuch make the case in detail. Richard Elliott Friedman in Who Wrote the Bible? gives the popular version. Even more conservative critical scholars like John Goldingay grant the multi-source compositional history while sometimes pushing back on the dating.

Some conservative scholars try a middle path. Kenneth Kitchen in On the Reliability of the Old Testament accepts substantial Mosaic-era material with later editorial activity. Duane Garrett pushes back on Wellhausen's specific dating but concedes editorial layering. The full "Moses wrote every word" position is essentially confined to Young-Earth-Creationist apologetics at this point.

Verdict: genuine and well-established contradiction between traditional Mosaic authorship and the textual evidence. Numbers 12:3 alone is a thin reed — the SAB undersells the case — but the cumulative evidence from doublets, anachronisms, divine names, and legal contradictions is overwhelming. That is the consensus of mainstream Hebrew Bible scholarship, with only the dating and exact source-divisions seriously debated.

contradictions.question: Who argued in favor of occupying Canaan during the Exodus?
contradictions.summary: Numbers 13:30 says only Caleb stilled the people and argued for going up to take the land. Numbers 14:6-9, just one chapter later, says both Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and argued for occupying the good land YHWH had promised.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here is sequential-events theory: Caleb spoke first and alone in Numbers 13:30, then both Joshua and Caleb spoke together in Numbers 14:6 after the people's negative reaction had escalated. The two passages describe different moments in the same crisis — Caleb's initial counter-speech, then the joint Joshua-Caleb intervention after the people threatened to stone Moses and return to Egypt. Gleason Archer, Walter Kaiser, and Timothy Ashley in his NICOT Numbers all run this argument, and it's not crazy. Numbers 13:30 occurs immediately after the spies' report, while Numbers 14:6 occurs after the congregation has begun rebelling — so a temporal-progression read is textually defensible.

The sequential-events reading does substantial work. The narrative arc moves from spy report, to Caleb's counter, to people's rebellion, to Joshua-and-Caleb's joint counter, to the divine judgment of forty years in the wilderness. So the two pro-occupation speeches can be read as escalating responses to escalating crisis, with Joshua joining only when things got worse.

Where the harmonization gets shakier is the source-critical evidence that Numbers 13-14 contain interwoven narratives from different traditions. Baruch Levine in his Anchor Bible Numbers and Jacob Milgrom in JPS Numbers identify clear seams. The list of spies in 13:1-16 is Priestly material with Joshua already named (and Hoshea renamed Joshua, 13:16), but the older JE narrative beneath shows signs of having only Caleb as the dissenting spy. Numbers 14:24 has YHWH single out Caleb alone ("my servant Caleb... him will I bring into the land"), with Joshua's exemption added separately at 14:30 in what most source critics treat as a Priestly insertion. Deuteronomy 1:36 also names only Caleb in its retelling — Joshua appears in Deuteronomy 1:38 in a separate notice. Joel Baden's The Composition of the Pentateuch traces these doublets carefully and argues the original tradition had Caleb as the sole faithful spy, with Joshua's pairing being a later Priestly editorial move that brings the future conquest leader into the wilderness-faithfulness narrative.

So the apologetic sequential read works as a literary harmonization of the final form, but the underlying compositional history points to two different traditions about who the faithful spy was, with Joshua added later. Verdict: weak-to-moderate contradiction. The final-form text can be harmonized as two consecutive moments in one crisis, but the source-critical evidence and the Deuteronomy-1 retelling suggest the original tradition knew only Caleb. The contradiction is more compositional than narrative.

contradictions.question: Should we follow our own hearts?
contradictions.summary: Ecclesiastes 11:9 tells the young to walk in the ways of their heart and the sight of their eyes. But Numbers 15:39 commands Israel not to seek after their own heart and eyes, and Proverbs 28:26 calls anyone who trusts his own heart a fool.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization here works the genre and rhetorical-mode angle. Ecclesiastes is wisdom literature operating in a particular voice — the Qoheleth's experimental, sometimes sardonic exploration of life under the sun. 11:9 specifically continues with "but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment," which most commentators read as either a sincere balancing clause or as Qoheleth's ironic deflation of the apparent permission. So the verse, read in context, isn't really a green light to follow your heart — it's a setup for a warning. Tremper Longman in his NICOT Ecclesiastes and Choon-Leong Seow in his Anchor Bible Ecclesiastes both treat 11:9 as either ironic or as immediately qualified by the judgment notice. So the contradiction softens considerably when you read past the cherry-picked clause.

This is actually the right read of Ecclesiastes 11:9, and most critical scholars agree. James Crenshaw in his Old Testament Library Ecclesiastes argues Qoheleth's apparent permissions are typically rhetorical setups for the larger frame's warnings about divine judgment and the limits of human knowledge. Michael Fox's *A Time to Tear Down and a Time to Build Up* makes the same case. So if the SAB framing is reading 11:9 as a free-for-all permission, that's a misread of the verse.

Where there's still some lingering tension is the broader Qoheleth voice itself. Even granting that 11:9 is qualified by judgment, Qoheleth as a whole offers a wisdom-skeptical perspective that sits in real tension with the Deuteronomic-prophetic main line — eat, drink, and be glad in your toil (3:13, 5:18-19, 8:15) is a pretty regular refrain, and the book's relationship to Torah obedience is famously complicated. Crenshaw and Choon-Leong Seow both note that Ecclesiastes was nearly excluded from the Hebrew canon (b. Shabbat 30b) precisely because the rabbis recognized this tension, and the conventional epilogue (12:13-14) was likely added by a later hand to bring the book into orthodoxy. So the underlying tension between Qohelethic wisdom-skepticism and Deuteronomic-prophetic obedience-ethics is genuine — but it's not really captured by the heart-following question.

Proverbs 28:26 vs. Ecclesiastes 11:9 isn't even a sharp pairing once you handle the genres carefully — they're both wisdom literature warning about the unreliability of the heart, just in different voices. Numbers 15:39 is a Priestly cultic-discipline text about not chasing after foreign worship by following the eyes, which is a narrower target than the SAB framing implies.

Verdict: weak contradiction. The apparent contradiction depends on reading Ecclesiastes 11:9 outside its immediate context. Read in full, the verse is closer to a warning than a permission. There's a real underlying tension between Qoheleth's voice and the Deuteronomic mainstream, but the heart-following framing doesn't really land it.

contradictions.question: What angered God so much that he didn't allow Moses to enter the promised land?
contradictions.summary: Numbers 20:7-12 says YHWH barred Moses and Aaron from the promised land because Moses struck the rock at Meribah twice instead of speaking to it as commanded — failing to sanctify YHWH before the people. But Deuteronomy 3:26-27 and 4:21 have Moses tell Israel YHWH was angry with him "for your sakes" — that is, because of the people's sin, not Moses'.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization is the both-and reading: Moses was punished for his own failure at Meribah AND that failure happened in the context of the people's provocation, so Deuteronomy's "for your sakes" language can mean "because of the situation you put me in." Eugene Merrill in his NAC Deuteronomy and Daniel Block in his NIVAC Deuteronomy both run this line. The rebellious complaining of the people in Numbers 20:2-5 is what set up the Meribah incident, so Moses can plausibly say later that the people's behavior contributed to his loss. Gleason Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties takes a similar tack.

This harmonization works at a high level. Deuteronomy 32:51 (in the same book, in the Song of Moses) does explicitly say Moses transgressed against YHWH at Meribah, so Deuteronomy itself doesn't deny Moses' personal failure. And the Hebrew bigelalkem in Deuteronomy 3:26 ("on your account" or "for your sakes") can plausibly mean "because of the situation you produced." So the plain-reading apparent contradiction softens once you read Deuteronomy as a whole rather than just the 3:26 verse in isolation.

Where the harmonization gets weaker is the rhetorical force of Deuteronomy 3:23-27 in context. Moses is recounting his pleading with YHWH and explicitly says "the LORD was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me." The whole rhetorical move is to deflect responsibility outward — to the people — not to confess his own failure. Deuteronomic Moses casts himself as the long-suffering leader bearing the consequences of the congregation's sin, which is in tension with the Numbers 20 portrait of a Moses who fails at the moment of testing. Source critics like Joel Baden and Thomas Dozeman argue the two passages reflect different traditions about why Moses didn't enter the land. The Priestly Numbers tradition needs to explain why even Moses fell short by giving him a specific covenant infraction (cf. similar concerns about Aaron's golden-calf failure in another Priestly handling). The Deuteronomic tradition, focused on the people's recurring rebellion as the great theological theme, attributes Moses' loss to the same pattern of communal disobedience.

There's also a deeper exegetical question about what exactly Moses did wrong at Meribah. The text says "because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel," which is vague. Did he strike instead of speak? Did he say "must we fetch you water" attributing the miracle to himself? Did he show anger rather than faith? Jacob Milgrom in his JPS Numbers catalogues the rabbinic options and notes the text doesn't actually specify. So Numbers 20 itself is somewhat ambiguous about the offense, which makes the comparison with Deuteronomy all the more strained.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The both-and harmonization is textually defensible if you grant that bigelalkem is broad enough to absorb Moses' own failure. The source-critical evidence points to two different traditions with different theological emphases — Priestly individual-failure versus Deuteronomic communal-failure — assembled side by side without full reconciliation.
